description_full: Lindsay Corporation, together with its subsidiaries, provides water management and road infrastructure products and services in the United States and internationally. It operates through two segments, Irrigation and Infrastructure. The Irrigation segment manufactures and markets center pivot, lateral move, and hose reel irrigation systems, as well as large diameter steel tubing and repair and replacement parts for its irrigation systems and controls under the Zimmatic, FieldNET, and FieldWise brands. This segment also offers industrial internet of things technology solutions, data acquisition and management systems, and custom electronic equipment for critical applications under the Elecsys brand; and contract manufacturing services, including contract manufacturing services, including steel tubing production, hot-dip galvanization, fabrication, welding, and related finishing and assembly services. Its Infrastructure segment provides Road Zipper System comprised of T-shaped concrete and steel barriers, barrier transfer machine, and variable length barriers, which are used for highway reconstruction, paving and resurfacing, road widening, median and shoulder construction, and repairs to tunnels and bridges. This segment also offers moveable barriers, specialty barriers, crash cushions and end terminals, road marking and road safety equipment, and railroad signals and structures. The company was founded in 1955 and is headquartered in Omaha, Nebraska.

financial_summary: Lindsay Corporation is a small-cap industrials business with a $1.1B market cap on $636M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -6% over the past three years and +2% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 17% against a 8% cost of capital, a 9-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, with gross margins sitting at 28%.

The business throws off $35M in free cash flow — roughly 5 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.35× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 48× is fortress-like.

Management returns a meaningful 8.8% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $75.0M (7% of market cap).

growth: Revenue has compounded at -6.2% over 3 years, 2.3% over 5 years and 2.1% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 16%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.

Capex runs 1.7x depreciation (6.3% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 7, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.3%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
